name: Rua Bioscience Limited
overview: Rua Bioscience is a Māori-founded, Tairāwhiti (Gisborne)-based medicinal cannabis company that has pivoted from a capital-intensive owned cultivation/manufacturing model to an asset-light genetics-and-distribution model, outsourcing cultivation and manufacturing to partners while selling New Zealand-grown cannabis genetics and products into Germany, Australia, the United Kingdom, Czechia and New Zealand. It is a pre-profitability, going-concern-qualified micro-cap: at a share price of roughly NZ$0.035 and ~338-339m shares on issue, market capitalisation is approximately NZ$11.5-11.8m, and the FY2025 audited accounts were issued with a disclaimer of opinion (following an identical disclaimer in FY2024) because the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to conclude the group can continue as a going concern.

business_model.summary: Rua no longer owns or operates significant cultivation or manufacturing infrastructure (its Gisborne GMP facility, built for ~NZ$4m, was closed in FY2023 and is now held for sale). The current model is capital-light: Rua supplies genetics and finished/branded medicinal cannabis products (oils and dried flower) through third-party distribution and clinic partners into Germany, Australia, the UK, Czechia and New Zealand, earning revenue from product sales rather than from vertically integrated growing/processing. Revenue is transactional (product sale, not subscription), heavily weighted toward B2B distributor/clinic-chain relationships that in turn reach B2C prescribing patients. Growth has been extremely fast off a tiny base: H1 FY2026 receipts from customers were NZ$1.33m versus NZ$0.53m in H1 FY2025 (+153%), and FY2025 full-year revenue from customers was NZ$1.51m versus just NZ$86k in FY2024 (+1,661%). Despite the growth, absolute revenue remains small relative to the cost base, and the company remains deeply loss-making (H1 FY2026 net loss NZ$1.79m; FY2025 net loss NZ$3.46m).

revenue_streams.name: Australia
revenue_streams.description: Sale of goods into Australian clinic chains and distributors, leveraging New Zealand legacy genetics (e.g. Rua Rau Hiwa T23 dried flower)
revenue_streams.share_or_importance: H1 FY2026: NZ$672k of NZ$1.334m total revenue (~50%), up from NZ$225k in H1 FY2025 — currently the largest single market

revenue_streams.name: New Zealand
revenue_streams.description: Domestic sale of medicinal cannabis products (four approved products as of H1 FY2026) via the NZ Medicinal Cannabis Scheme
revenue_streams.share_or_importance: H1 FY2026: NZ$536k (~40%), up from NZ$184k in H1 FY2025; smaller in absolute scale but central to brand identity and the Compassionate Access Programme

revenue_streams.name: Other international markets (Germany, UK, Czechia)
revenue_streams.description: Product sold via distribution partners: Nimbus Health (Germany, 3-year extended distribution agreement), Target Healthcare (UK, launched Dec-2024) and Motagon (Czechia/Poland, launched Sept-2025). A separate, larger UK clinic/distribution agreement signed July 2026 (post-period) is expected to generate NZ$10m+ of revenue over its initial two-year term — a scale step-change versus anything reported to date
revenue_streams.share_or_importance: H1 FY2026: NZ$126k (~10%) in the reported 'other international' line, but this predates the July 2026 UK deal, which if it delivers as contracted would become the dominant revenue driver

business_model.customer_type: B2B — distributors, pharmacies and clinic chains in each market, which then serve prescribing doctors and patients (B2C end-demand, but Rua's direct customers are commercial partners, not patients)
business_model.geographic_mix: H1 FY2026 revenue: Australia ~50%, New Zealand ~40%, other international (Germany/UK/Czechia combined) ~10%; single reportable operating segment (R&D and sale of pharmaceutical products in NZ, Europe and Australia) per NZ IFRS 8

main_competitors: Cann Group (ASX-listed, Australia — Rua's former litigation counterparty, now a supply partner)
Canadian LPs exporting into Germany (Canada supplies ~53% of Germany's ~200 tonnes/year import volume, led by players such as Tilray, Canopy Growth and Aurora Cannabis subsidiaries)
Portuguese/European cultivators (Portugal is the second-largest source of German imports and a lower-cost, EU-GMP-proximate processing hub)
Numerous smaller Australian medicinal cannabis brands competing for the same clinic-chain shelf space amid a TGA review of high-volume telehealth prescribing
Larger, better-capitalised global cannabis companies with far greater cultivation scale and lower unit costs
competitive_position.market_position: Sub-scale, niche participant. Rua's ~NZ$11.5m market capitalisation is a rounding error next to the multi-hundred-million-dollar Canadian, European and Australian producers that dominate the German and Australian import markets by volume. Rua has no meaningful share of either the German (~200 tonnes/year import market, FY25 estimated at >€500m) or Australian (~A$650m) medicinal cannabis markets; its positioning is as a tiny, differentiated niche brand rather than a volume competitor.

moat_factors.factor: New Zealand / Tairāwhiti / Māori provenance branding
moat_factors.description: Rua markets legacy New Zealand genetics and an authentic Māori-founded origin story (Rau Hiwa T23, positioned as derived from distinctive, community-held genetics) as differentiation in increasingly commoditised, price-competitive import markets. This is a genuine point of difference in marketing terms — very few competitors can credibly claim indigenous-community provenance — but it is unproven as a durable price/volume advantage at scale, and management's own language ('offering clear differentiation in a very competitive market') concedes the market is fundamentally commoditised. It should be read as a real but modest brand asset, not a structural barrier to entry, since genetics can in principle be propagated and grown elsewhere, and clinic/prescriber decisions are heavily influenced by price and consistent supply, not provenance narrative alone.

moat_factors.factor: Existing distribution relationships (Nimbus Health, Target Healthcare, Motagon, and the July-2026 undisclosed large UK partner)
moat_factors.description: Multi-year exclusive or preferred distribution agreements provide near-term revenue visibility and market access that would take years to rebuild, but these are commercial contracts terminable/renewable on normal business terms, not durable structural moats, and depend entirely on Rua continuing to supply competitively priced, reliably available product.

Rua has navigated NZ Medicinal Cannabis Scheme approval for four products and built compliance relationships across multiple jurisdictions (Germany, UK, Australia, Czechia), which is a genuine (if modest) barrier for a brand-new entrant, but is matched or exceeded by every established competitor of scale.

As an outsourced-cultivation, sub-scale exporter, Rua has no cost advantage versus larger integrated Canadian or European producers; if anything it is structurally cost-disadvantaged, which is dangerous given that German import prices are compressing sharply (average price/gram trending from ~€5 toward ~€4 by late 2026) and 'cost of production is becoming the decisive competitive factor'

weaknesses: No cultivation or manufacturing cost advantage — Rua deliberately exited owned production and is now a price-taking distributor/brand-owner competing against integrated, lower-cost Canadian and Portuguese suppliers into a German market experiencing rapid price compression from oversupply
Extreme sub-scale versus every meaningful competitor in its target markets — a ~NZ$11.5m company cannot match the capital, R&D or distribution reach of ASX/TSX-listed medicinal cannabis producers

Revenue concentration risk in a small number of distribution partners per market (Nimbus in Germany, Target Healthcare and now a single large unnamed UK partner, Motagon in Czechia/Poland) — loss of any one partner would be a material revenue shock

Company-wide financial fragility (see Financial Risks) undermines its ability to guarantee reliable, at-scale supply to partners, which is precisely what large clinic chains and distributors need most from a supplier

'New Zealand grown' and Māori-provenance positioning is a genuine story but is unlikely to command a durable price premium once international clinic buyers optimise purely on cost and consistency of supply, particularly in the German market's current oversupply/price-war dynamic

growth_drivers: July 2026 UK distribution agreement with a large, unnamed UK clinic/distribution business — Rua's largest-ever export deal, expected to generate NZ$10m+ of revenue over its initial two-year term (versus ~NZ$2.9m total FY2025 revenue+income), which if delivered would be transformative relative to the company's current scale

Continued fast (though small-base) revenue growth across all key markets: H1 FY2026 customer receipts +153% YoY; New Zealand grown product launched into Germany August 2025; product entry into Czechia (Sept 2025) and the UK (Dec 2024) both still ramping

Halving-and-still-falling operating cash burn: net operating cash outflow improved from NZ$1.94m (H1 FY2025) to NZ$1.52m (H1 FY2026), suggesting the capital-light pivot and cost discipline are working, at least directionally

Pending sale of the Gisborne manufacturing facility (leasehold buildings plus extraction/manufacturing equipment, carried at ~NZ$0.86m net) — proceeds are explicitly relied upon by the Board as part of the going-concern case, and a successful sale would both retire secured debt and inject net cash

New Zealand genetics licensed to Apollo Green for cultivation in Canada (April 2026) and trial crops planned in NZ and Australia — an early, low-capital way to monetise Rua's genetic IP beyond direct product export

Regulatory tailwinds still developing in several markets: German 2024 reform continues to broaden prescribing access; Czechia allowed GP prescribing from April 2025; UK medicinal cannabis patient numbers are projected to exceed 140,000 in 2026 with import volumes doubling to 30,000kg+, and the market remains almost entirely import-dependent

business.description: A small number of exclusive or near-exclusive distribution relationships per geography (Nimbus in Germany, the new unnamed UK partner, Motagon in Czechia/Poland) mean the loss, renegotiation, or underperformance of any single partner would materially impair revenue in that market

business.risk: No cost/scale moat in a price-compressing market
business.description: Rua is an outsourced-production, brand/genetics-led exporter competing against integrated, lower-cost Canadian and Portuguese suppliers in Germany, where average selling prices are compressing toward ~€4/gram by late 2026 amid oversupply — a structurally difficult backdrop for a sub-scale, higher-relative-cost new entrant

business.risk: Execution risk on the July 2026 UK deal
business.description: The NZ$10m/2-year UK agreement is unaudited, forward-looking and with an undisclosed partner; delivery depends on Rua's ability to supply reliably at the volumes and price required, which is uncertain given the company's own liquidity constraints
Even after 1,661% FY2025 revenue growth, customer revenue was only NZ$1.51m for the full year — the business remains pre-scale and highly sensitive to any single order timing or customer loss

financial.risk: Going concern — explicitly acknowledged material uncertainty
financial.description: The H1 FY2026 accounts state plainly that 'material uncertainties continue to exist that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern.' The Board's ability to continue trading is explicitly contingent on (i) achieving forecast revenue growth, (ii) completing the sale of the Gisborne facility, and (iii) if needed, further equity raising. This is not boilerplate — the FY2025 audit disclaimer (see Regulatory Risks) shows the auditor itself could not get comfortable with the same forecasts a few months earlier.

financial.risk: Continuing cash burn against a thin cash base
financial.description: Net operating cash outflow of NZ$1.52m in H1 FY2026 (NZ$1.94m in H1 FY2025) against cash and equivalents of only NZ$2.17m at 31 December 2025 (up from a critically low NZ$241k at 30 June 2025 only because of the December 2025 capital raise) — the company is persistently burning cash faster than it can be confident of replacing organically

financial.risk: Serial, deeply dilutive equity raising at a collapsing share price
financial.description: Shares on issue rose from 159.75m (30 Jun 2024) to 223.65m (30 Jun 2025) to 338.04m (31 Dec 2025) to ~339.4m (Aug 2026) — a +112% increase in 18 months and continuing. Recent capital has been raised at deeply discounted prices (the Nov-2024 rights offer priced at $0.025, a 47.9% discount to VWAP; new debt-facility warrants issued in 2026 carry a $0.015 exercise price, below even today's ~$0.035 share price). Accumulated losses of NZ$42.76m against total share capital raised of NZ$48.17m mean the company has already consumed roughly 89% of all capital ever contributed by shareholders. At the current tick-floor-adjacent price, each further raise mechanically transfers a very large share of the company to new money and existing holders who do not participate are diluted severely.

As at 31 December 2025, borrowings had risen to NZ$1.77m (from NZ$0.73m at 30 June 2025), comprising short-term lending, inventory finance, and supplier finance arrangements — several carrying embedded equity conversion or warrant features (e.g. a loan renegotiated in December 2025 with a VWAP-linked conversion option). This is expensive, short-tenor, related-party-linked financing (two directors are inventory-finance lenders) rather than conventional bank debt, indicating restricted access to cheaper capital

financial.risk: Balance sheet has been comprehensively written down
financial.description: Total assets fell from NZ$30.9m (FY2021) to NZ$7.7m (FY2024) and equity from NZ$28.8m (FY2021) to NZ$5.84m (H1 FY2026), reflecting an FY2024 goodwill/PP&E impairment of ~NZ$8.5m+ following the failed owned-cultivation strategy; residual goodwill of NZ$2.19m still on the balance sheet at 31 December 2025 depends on forecasts the auditor has twice been unable to corroborate

regulatory.risk: FY2025 disclaimer of opinion by PwC — the second consecutive year
regulatory.description: PwC's report on the 30 June 2025 financial statements is a disclaimer of opinion, not merely a qualified opinion or emphasis of matter — the most severe outcome available under NZ/international auditing standards, meaning the auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to form any opinion at all. The stated basis: without an additional capital raise the Group would not have sufficient cash for 12 months, and the auditor could not corroborate the going-concern basis or the recoverability of NZ$2.19m goodwill, NZ$2.14m PP&E, NZ$0.06m right-of-use assets and NZ$0.89m assets-held-for-sale (NZ$5.29m combined) underpinning those forecasts. Critically, the 30 June 2024 financial statements also carried a disclaimer of opinion — this is now a two-year pattern, not a one-off, and there is no evidence as of August 2026 that the FY2026 audit (due imminently, given the 30 June fiscal year-end) will avoid a third consecutive disclaimer.

Germany's medicinal cannabis import volumes have surged (Q1 2026 imports revised up to 67.6 tonnes, full 2025 imports ~200-201 tonnes, Canada alone supplying ~53%), and increased competition/oversupply is compressing average prices toward ~€4/gram by late 2026, making production cost the decisive competitive factor — a dynamic Rua, as an outsourced-production, sub-scale exporter, is poorly positioned to win on

regulatory.risk: Australian TGA tightening on prescribing channels
regulatory.description: The TGA opened a formal review of medicinal cannabis safety and prescribing in August 2025, and Ahpra has issued guidance targeting high-volume telehealth prescribing; tighter rules through 2026-2027 could compress the clinic-chain/telehealth prescribing channel that is currently Rua's largest revenue source (~50% of H1 FY2026 revenue)

Rua must simultaneously satisfy NZ Medicinal Cannabis Scheme, German narcotics/prescribing rules, UK MHRA/clinic requirements, Australian TGA pathways (Special Access Scheme/Authorised Prescriber/ARTG) and Czech/Polish requirements — a disproportionate compliance burden for a company of this size, with each jurisdiction able to independently disrupt a revenue stream

macro.description: Revenue is earned across NZD, EUR (Germany, Czechia), GBP (UK) and AUD (Australia) while costs are substantially NZD-denominated; currency translation losses of NZ$40,686 were recorded in H1 FY2026 alone, and a company this cash-constrained has little capacity to hedge

macro.risk: Global capital markets appetite for loss-making micro-cap cannabis equities
macro.description: Rua's ability to keep raising the equity capital its own going-concern statement depends on is directly exposed to broader risk appetite for speculative, cash-burning small caps; a market downturn or cannabis-sector sentiment reversal would directly threaten its ability to fund itself

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global medicinal cannabis demand is genuinely growing — Germany's import market has grown from roughly 19-80 tonnes in H1 2025 alone to ~200+ tonnes annualised, the UK market is projected to exceed 140,000 patients with import volumes doubling toward 30,000kg in 2026, and Australia remains a large (~A$650m), actively growing market with 4.5m units prescribed in 2024. However, this growth is increasingly a race to the bottom on price as global supply (led by Canada and, in Europe, Portugal) scales faster than demand, with German average prices trending from ~€5 toward ~€4/gram by late 2026 — a genuinely tough backdrop for a small, higher-cost New Zealand exporter without production scale.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low direct macroeconomic cyclicality (healthcare/prescription demand is relatively defensive), but extremely high company-specific financing cyclicality — Rua's survival is tied to capital markets access, not consumer spending cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Indirect but material: higher rates raise the cost of Rua's short-term/inventory finance facilities and reduce risk appetite for speculative micro-cap equity raises, both of which matter disproportionately for a company that must repeatedly access external capital to survive
key_input_costs: Third-party cultivation and manufacturing (outsourced, cost pass-through)
International freight/logistics for cross-border pharmaceutical-grade shipments
Cost of capital (increasingly expensive as equity dilutes and debt carries warrant/conversion sweeteners)

recent_developments.significance: Cited by the Board as one of the key operational proof-points supporting the FY2026 going-concern assessment

recent_developments.event: First dried flower products launched into Czechia via distribution partner Motagon, following April 2025 Czech regulatory reform allowing GP prescribing
recent_developments.significance: Early-stage new-market entry; contributed only a small part of the NZ$126k 'other international markets' H1 FY2026 revenue line

recent_developments.event: Pro-rata 1-for-3 renounceable rights offer plus placement of oversubscription, raising NZ$2,022,750 net of costs; 92.6m shares issued 18 December 2025 plus a further 16.8m shares issued Aug/Sept 2025 for short-term working capital and 5.0m shares as staff share-based payment — combined FY2026-H1 dilution of 114.4m new shares (+51% of the opening share count)
recent_developments.significance: The primary source of the liquidity improvement that allowed the Board to continue applying the going-concern basis in the H1 FY2026 accounts; also the latest instalment in a pattern of ~annual, deeply dilutive capital raises

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026 (six months to 31 December 2025) results signed: net loss NZ$1.79m, net operating cash outflow NZ$1.52m (improved from NZ$1.94m H1 FY2025), cash NZ$2.17m, going concern material uncertainty explicitly disclosed and made contingent on revenue forecasts and the Gisborne facility sale
recent_developments.significance: Confirms the going-concern qualification persists into FY2026 following the FY2025 disclaimer of opinion

recent_developments.significance: A low-capital way to monetise genetic IP beyond direct product export; financial terms not disclosed in available sources

recent_developments.significance: A potential scale step-change if delivered — more than 3x FY2025's total revenue and other income (NZ$1.9m) per year on average — but unaudited, forward-looking, and dependent on Rua's ability to reliably supply an undisclosed partner at scale

recent_developments.event: New warrants (670,794) issued at a $0.015 exercise price as part of a debt-facility roll-over, taking total warrants on issue to 8,733,456; ordinary shares on issue ~339.4m
recent_developments.significance: Confirms continuing reliance on warrant-sweetened short-term debt facilities and a share count still expanding modestly post-H1

recent_developments.significance: The stock trades near its all-time tick-floor range, meaning further capital raises — which the going-concern statement makes explicitly conditional — would be severely dilutive to existing holders

recent_developments.significance: Standard governance calendar item; no signalled change of board composition beyond ordinary re-election

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Results, signed 26 February 2026 (plus 16 July 2026 UK export deal announcement)

items.target: No numeric revenue or profitability target disclosed; qualitative dependency on 'achieving revenue forecasts' plus successful completion of the Gisborne facility sale plus, if needed, further equity raising
items.vs_prior: maintained — same conditional going-concern framing as FY2025 (disclaimer of opinion) and H1 FY2025
items.notes: The Board states explicitly: 'Should the Group be unsuccessful in achieving its revenue forecasts, or if actual revenue growth is lower than projected, the proceeds from the sale of the facility are less than expected the Group may be unable to manage its minimum cash expenditure requirements.' No specific revenue, margin or breakeven-date figures are disclosed in the extracted filings.

items.target: More than NZ$10 million over an initial two-year term
items.vs_prior: n/a — first disclosure of this contract
items.notes: Unaudited, contract-based forward figure from a single undisclosed customer; not yet reflected in any reported financial period

items.target: Sale and settlement of the Gisborne manufacturing/leasehold facility to a currently unidentified buyer; proceeds first applied to the secured building loan (including accrued interest and a NZ$100,000 bullet payment) with net proceeds available to the Group thereafter
items.period: No specific completion date given; 'actively engaged with a number of interested parties' as at 26 February 2026
items.vs_prior: maintained — has been 'in progress' across multiple reporting periods without confirmed completion
items.notes: Directly load-bearing for the going-concern conclusion; failure or delay would be a significant negative catalyst

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Paul Naske on the July 2026 UK deal: 'This agreement represents an extremely important milestone in Rua's international growth strategy and further validates the quality and uniqueness of our New Zealand-grown product offering.' In the FY2025 Annual Report, Chair Anna Stove and CEO Paul Naske described FY25 as marking 'a pivotal shift... from setting the right strategy to executing it' and stated 'the extraordinary is in our grasp,' while acknowledging FY25 loss before tax of NZ$3.46m was 'in line with expectations.' No FY2026 or FY2027 numeric revenue, margin or breakeven guidance has been located in the available filings or subsequent announcements; all forward commentary is qualitative.

bull_case: Revenue is compounding fast off a genuinely tiny base — customer receipts +153% YoY in H1 FY2026 and +1,661% in FY2025 — while operating cash burn has fallen materially (NZ$1.94m to NZ$1.52m half-on-half), a combination that, if sustained, plausibly reaches operating breakeven within a small number of further half-years

The asset-light genetics-and-distribution pivot removed the capital intensity (and impairment risk) of owned cultivation/manufacturing, meaning any further revenue growth should flow through to margin far more efficiently than under the old owned-facility model

Genuine, differentiated access to Europe's largest medicinal cannabis market (Germany) plus fast-growing UK, Czech and Australian channels, capped by a July 2026 UK deal that — if it delivers even a fraction of its stated NZ$10m/two-year potential — would be transformative relative to the company's current ~NZ$11.5m market cap and sub-NZ$2m annual revenue base

The Māori/Tairāwhiti provenance and legacy New Zealand genetics story is a real, hard-to-replicate brand asset (not available to Canadian or Portuguese bulk producers) that has demonstrably supported product uptake (e.g. Rau Hiwa T23 in Australia) and differentiates Rua in what is otherwise a commoditising market
A successful Gisborne facility sale would simultaneously retire secured debt and inject net cash, directly addressing the single largest near-term liquidity risk the Board has flagged
bear_case: This is a going-concern situation, not merely a high-risk growth stock: PwC issued a disclaimer of opinion — the most severe audit outcome available — on the FY2025 accounts, following an identical disclaimer on FY2024, and the H1 FY2026 accounts state plainly that material uncertainties continue to exist that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern. The relevant bear-case outcome is permanent loss of capital via insolvency or a forced fire-sale wind-down, not merely share-price underperformance.

The company has already consumed roughly 89% of all capital ever raised from shareholders (NZ$42.76m of accumulated losses against NZ$48.17m of share capital raised) and shares on issue have more than doubled in 18 months (159.75m to ~339.4m); at a ~NZ$0.035 share price near the practical tick floor, each further raise is enormously dilutive, and continuing new warrant issuance at a $0.015 strike (below the current share price) shows the trend is ongoing, not resolved

Going concern is explicitly conditional on two things outside full company control — hitting revenue growth forecasts and completing the Gisborne facility sale to an as-yet-unidentified buyer — and if either falls short, 'the Group may be unable to manage its minimum cash expenditure requirements' in the Board's own words

Rua has no cost or scale moat and is entering a German market experiencing sharp price compression (average prices trending toward ~€4/gram by late 2026) driven by Canadian- and Portuguese-led oversupply — a dangerous combination for a sub-scale, higher-cost, outsourced-production exporter whose main differentiation is a brand story rather than a production-cost advantage

The business remains critically dependent on a handful of distribution partners per market (several undisclosed or newly signed), on continued shareholder goodwill to fund an ~annual rights-issue cadence, and on management/Board revenue forecasts that the company's own auditor has twice, in successive years, been unable to corroborate

moat_rating.justification: Rua's only genuine points of differentiation — Māori/Tairāwhiti provenance, legacy New Zealand cannabis genetics, and existing distribution relationships in Germany, the UK, Australia and Czechia — are real but narrow and largely unprotected by structural barriers. It has no cost advantage (it deliberately exited owned cultivation), no scale advantage (it is a sub-NZ$15m company competing against multi-hundred-million-dollar Canadian, Portuguese and Australian producers), no meaningful switching costs locking in its distribution partners, and no regulatory protection unavailable to competitors. In a German market now defined by price compression driven by lower-cost integrated overseas suppliers, brand/provenance narrative alone is unlikely to be sufficient competitive protection. The moat question is, in any case, secondary to the going-concern question: a company whose survival is explicitly conditioned on hitting revenue forecasts and completing an asset sale is not best analysed primarily through a moat lens.

management_assessment: CEO Paul Naske (promoted from within in February 2023) and Chair Anna Stove (a director since 2019, chair since 2023, ex-GlaxoSmithKline NZ General Manager) have executed a credible strategic pivot — closing the capital-intensive Gisborne manufacturing operation, resolving litigation with Cann Group into a supply agreement, and driving fast (if small-base) revenue growth across four-plus export markets while materially reducing the cash burn rate. This is genuine, competent operational execution under very difficult financial constraints. However, the persistent need for near-annual, deeply dilutive capital raises, the second consecutive year of an audit disclaimer of opinion, and a going-concern statement that is explicitly conditional on forecasts management itself sets, together indicate that management's ability to control the company's destiny is limited — survival depends as much on external capital markets goodwill and a successful asset sale as on operational execution. The board is independent-majority and stable (three of four directors standing for ordinary re-election at the October 2026 AGM, no signalled departures), which is a mild positive for governance credibility in a company this financially stressed.

dividend_profile.policy: No dividend paid or contemplated. Rua is loss-making, cash-constrained, and going-concern-qualified; all available cash (including capital raise proceeds) is directed to funding operations.
dividend_profile.current_yield_and_recent_history: Nil — the company has never paid a dividend since its 2021 NZX listing and is not expected to for the foreseeable future given its financial position.
dividend_profile.sustainability_assessment: Not applicable; a dividend is inconceivable until the company reaches sustained profitability and rebuilds its balance sheet, which the Board's own going-concern disclosure indicates is not assured even at the operating level.

valuation_context.framing: Rua should not be valued on conventional earnings, cash flow, or asset multiples — it has negative earnings, negative operating cash flow, and an audit disclaimer of opinion on its balance sheet's asset carrying values (goodwill, PP&E, held-for-sale assets totalling ~NZ$5.3m at 30 June 2025). At a ~NZ$11.5-11.8m market capitalisation against FY2025 total revenue and other income of just NZ$1.9m and an FY2025 net loss of NZ$3.46m, the market is pricing in either (a) a reasonable probability of insolvency/wind-down within the current going-concern uncertainty window, largely offset by (b) optionality value from the fast revenue growth trajectory and the July 2026 UK deal. This is fundamentally a binary, options-like situation rather than a business that can be meaningfully DCF'd or multiple-based: if revenue growth continues to compound, the facility sale completes, and the UK deal delivers even partially, the equity could be worth a multiple of its current ~NZ$11.5m market cap on a scarcity/re-rating basis; if any of the going-concern conditions fail, equity value could go to zero or near-zero via insolvency or forced administration.
valuation_context.historical_multiple_context: Not meaningful — the company has never generated a profit or positive free cash flow in the periods covered by the extracted filings (FY2021-H1 FY2026), and its asset base has been comprehensively impaired (total assets fell from NZ$30.9m in FY2021 to NZ$7.7m in FY2024 and equity from NZ$28.8m to NZ$5.8m over the same broad window), so no historical earnings or book-value multiple provides a useful valuation anchor.

investment_summary: Rua Bioscience is a distressed, pre-profitability medicinal cannabis micro-cap whose FY2025 accounts were issued with an auditor's disclaimer of opinion — the most severe audit outcome available — for the second consecutive year, and whose most recent (H1 FY2026) accounts explicitly disclose material uncertainty over the Group's ability to continue as a going concern, contingent on hitting revenue-growth forecasts and completing a facility sale to a buyer not yet identified. The company has already consumed roughly 89% of all capital ever raised from shareholders and has more than doubled its share count in 18 months through a pattern of near-annual, deeply discounted rights issues and placements, with warrant strikes as low as $0.015 continuing to be issued in 2026 — a dynamic that, at a ~NZ$0.035 share price near the practical tick floor, means each further capital raise severely dilutes existing holders. This is the dominant investment consideration and should not be minimised: the relevant downside scenario is permanent loss of capital via insolvency or terminal dilution, not merely underperformance. Set against this, the operational story is genuinely improving: an asset-light pivot away from owned cultivation/manufacturing, fast (if small-base) revenue growth (+153% H1 FY2026, +1,661% FY2025), materially reduced half-on-half cash burn, and a July 2026 UK distribution agreement potentially worth more than NZ$10m over two years that would be transformative relative to the company's current scale. Rua's competitive position rests on a real but narrow moat — Māori/Tairāwhiti provenance and legacy New Zealand genetics — operating in markets (particularly Germany) that are becoming more price-competitive as lower-cost Canadian and Portuguese supply floods in, which is a genuinely difficult backdrop for a sub-scale, outsourced-production exporter. For prospective investors, this is best understood as a highly asymmetric, options-like security: a plausible route to a multiple of the current ~NZ$11.5m market capitalisation if the revenue trajectory, facility sale and UK deal all land as hoped, against a real and openly disclosed risk of the equity being wiped out or diluted to near-nothing if any one of those pillars fails. It is not a conventional growth or value holding and should be sized accordingly.
